Every artist who walks into my office at twenty wants to argue about the percentage. That is the number they have heard about, and it feels like the number that decides whether the deal is fair. It is not. The term is the number that decides everything, and almost nobody argues about it. A bad percentage for two years costs you very little. A fair percentage for ten years can cost you a career, because the ten years will not be the ten years you expected them to be. Then there is the renewal clause. It is legal, it is normal, and it survives because the person signing it is usually twenty and is being told, honestly and correctly, that everybody signs the same thing. Nobody is lying to her. It is simply that the sentence that matters is written the way sentences are written when nobody expects them to be read out loud. And here is the part that people find hardest to believe. In almost every deal there is one specific day when the leverage changes hands, and neither side notices it at the time. The artist starts earning more than she costs. From that morning on, the label needs her more than she needs the label, and everything after that is a negotiation about a fact that both sides already know.

I was nineteen and everybody in that room was kind to me. That is the part people never get. There was no pressure, nobody rushed me, and if I had asked for a week to think about it, I am sure they would have given it to me. I did not ask. Asking would have looked like I did not trust them, and they had just told me they loved the record. So I read the percentage, and I understood the percentage perfectly, and I signed. What I did not understand was that three years would renew themselves unless I sat down and wrote a letter, at a date I would have to remember, six years before I would have any reason to remember it. Nobody said that part out loud. It was in there. I am not saying anybody hid it. If somebody had read it to me in that room, in the room, I would not be in this situation now. What would I tell somebody who is nineteen this year? Not to be braver. Bravery is not the problem, and it was never the problem. Take the contract home. Then ask one boring question, and ask it about every deal you are ever offered: what has to happen for this to end?

The mistake most people make about leverage is to treat it as a property of a person, when in fact it is a property of a moment. The same two people, with the same skills and the same lawyers, can swap positions entirely without either of them changing at all, simply because the thing one of them controls has stopped being scarce. That is what makes long contracts dangerous, and it is what has been happening across the music industry for fifteen years. Distribution has changed beyond recognition. An artist can now reach an audience without a label, without a shop, and without anybody's permission, which was unthinkable when most of these agreements were drafted. What has not changed is the length of the contracts. They were written for a world in which the label owned the only road to the listener, and they are still being signed, at the same length, in a world where it does not. We put that to a researcher who has spent twenty years studying how agreements fail. Her answer was blunt. A contract long enough to outlive the reason it was signed will end up in a room with a mediator in it, she said, and the only real question is whether the two sides get there while there is still any goodwill left to spend.
